analysis.one_liner: Creates a government office that manufactures and sells cheap generic versions of overpriced drugs, including insulin.
analysis.headline: Introduced in December 2018 with no cosponsors, the bill was referred to the Senate health committee and never advanced; it died when that Congress ended in January 2019 without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created an Office of Drug Manufacturing inside the Department of Health and Human Services. The office would manufacture and sell generic versions of drugs that are expensive, in shortage, or made by only one or two companies — with insulin production required within a year. The office would set a fair price for what it makes, sell its FDA approvals to private companies on the condition they keep prices low, and bar former drug-company lobbyists and executives of companies under federal enforcement from working there for six years. The bill was referred to committee and never got a hearing or a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who rely on overpriced off-patent drugs — especially insulin users — plus taxpayers, since Medicare and Medicaid would pay the fair price instead of inflated ones. Publicly manufactured drugs would create competition in markets with only one or two producers, and patients hit by shortages would gain a guaranteed public supply.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients paying high prices for old drugs

how_it_helps.text: It creates a public drug manufacturer to increase competition, lower prices, and address shortages of prescription drugs, including insulin.

It targets drugs with expired patents that are sold at high prices, are in shortage, or are made by fewer than three manufacturers — the categories of drugs where patients face the worst prices and access problems.
It requires public manufacturing of insulin within one year of enactment, aimed at the skyrocketing insulin prices patients pay.
It bars former drug-company lobbyists and former executives of drug companies under federal enforcement actions from working in the new office for six years.

analysis.who_pays: Drug manufacturers — especially those selling off-patent drugs at prices above what public manufacturing costs — would face a government competitor selling at cost-based "fair" prices. Taxpayers would fund the office's startup, though sales revenue would replenish it.

drawbacks.text: The government would set a 'fair price' for the drugs it makes, and if a private buyer of a publicly developed drug application raises the price above that fair price (adjusted for inflation), the government revokes the buyer's approval and resumes production itself — a substantial government role in a private market.

The Office must be making at least 15 drugs within a year of enactment and 25 within three years, an aggressive timeline for building manufacturing capacity and winning FDA approvals from a standing start.
Selling publicly developed drug applications back to private companies at three years could let them capture products taxpayers funded to manufacture.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit is large: direct public competition could force down prices for older drugs whose high prices and shortages are well documented, and the bill's revolving-door and conflict-of-interest bans are unusually strict. The drawbacks are that building a government manufacturer from scratch is untested and expensive, that setting a "fair price" would put pricing power in the hands of a federal office, and that a one-size-fits-all fair price could discourage investment in new generics. The bill never received a committee hearing, so none of these trade-offs were weighed on the record.

outcome.mechanism: Warren introduced it alone in the Senate's final weeks; it was referred to the health committee and died there with no hearing or vote when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on December 18, 2018, two weeks before the 115th Congress ended.
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which took no further action on it.
No senator signed on as a cosponsor.
The bill would have had HHS manufacture 15 drugs within a year and 25 within three years, including insulin within a year, and sell them at a 'fair price'.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmaceutical manufacturers keep their current pricing power on off-patent drugs and insulin, unchallenged by a public competitor. Patients and taxpayers continue paying the higher prices.

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the final two weeks of the 115th Congress and referred it to the Senate health committee.

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No one besides the sponsor ever took a position: with zero cosponsors and no committee action or vote, the record shows no stated support or opposition from either party.

industries.note: The bill would have the government directly compete with manufacturers of off-patent drugs, manufacture insulin within a year, and sell cheaply manufactured ingredients to generic competitors — undercutting monopoly pricing. Manufacturers of the targeted drugs stand to lose revenue and pricing power.
The bill bans former drug-industry lobbyists from working at the new public manufacturing office for six years, closing a revolving door.
